sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust is closing the captive bird programme at Castle Espie in County Down. Remaining captive birds will move to other UK sites from November, reducing the collection from around 500 to fewer than 100 birds. Guided school tours are also ending.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Avian influenza, cost-cutting, and Brexit transport difficulties caused the decline. Post-Brexit bio-security checks and export certificates created heavy administrative and logistical costs due to a lack of an aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK.

gist: Author Elif Shafak discusses her new novel, In One Brief Moment All Eternity.
The book fictionalises Gustave Flaubert's life, exploring creativity amidst global and personal crisis.
Living in self-imposed exile in London, Shafak reflects on artistic freedom and storytelling.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Novelist Elif Shafak has released her latest book, In One Brief Moment All Eternity, a fictionalised account of Gustave Flaubert's life. The work developed from Shafak questioning the value of creative writing during periods of conflict, division and technological change, alongside her personal struggles with depression and anxiety. She reimagines Flaubert's life through the perspectives of several women connected to him, blending the European novel tradition with Middle Eastern oral storytelling. Shafak noted striking parallels between her own experiences and Flaubert's, including feelings of childhood isolation and having their literary works prosecuted in court.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Shafak, now based in London in self-imposed exile, highlighted the vital necessity of free imagination and free speech. Having experienced trials, investigations and severe backlash in Turkey over her writing and identity, she views literature as one of the final remaining democratic spaces. For Shafak, storytelling slows individuals down to encourage mutual listening, asserting that the art of the novel transcends regional boundaries to express a shared humanity.

She sought to explore the value and role of creativity during times of crisis.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Policymakers from over one hundred countries met in Bangkok for the IMF annual meeting. Discussions focused on the unexpected strength of the global economy despite oil prices and geopolitical chaos. However, the IMF warned that resilience has come at a high cost, noting soaring public debt and expensive energy support measures. Meanwhile, stock markets in Asia and the US experienced turbulence amid growing fears over debt-financed AI investments.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Advanced economies face record budget deficits and rising government debt, leaving fiscal buffers depleted. The IMF cautions that governments may struggle to sustain costly energy subsidies and absorb future economic shocks. Additionally, heavy borrowing and leverage used to fund the artificial intelligence boom create systemic risks of a major market crash.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The IMF urged governments to tighten their public finances and implement temporary, targeted measures rather than broad subsidies. The UK is set to take over the G20 presidency next year, facing the challenge of rekindling multilateral cooperation amid deep global divisions.

timeline.text: ‘Keep away from the doctor’: a visit to an influencer’s wellness event, where the advice could kill

gist: An undercover reporter attended a wellness conference held by the controversial wellness influencer Barbara O'Neill.
O'Neill gave unscientific medical advice, telling attendees to avoid doctors, vaccines and treatments for serious illnesses.
Medical experts warned that her dangerous and unregulated recommendations risk causing severe harm or death.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Australian wellness influencer Barbara O'Neill hosted a five-day residential retreat in Cheshire where she advised attendees to avoid conventional medical treatments. Despite being banned from providing health services in Australia in 2019 for misleading vulnerable people, she offered unscientific remedies for conditions including lupus, a stomach tumour, glaucoma and thyroid dysfunction. An undercover reporter observed her dismissing antibiotics, vaccines and scientifically proven cancer treatments.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Prominent doctors and medical experts have warned that O'Neill's advice is dangerous and could lead to life-threatening illness or death. By encouraging followers to reject medical tests, ignore oncologists, and stop taking essential medications such as thyroxine and metformin, her teachings pose a significant risk to public health and safety.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Despite facing criticism from medical experts and a previous ban in Australia, O'Neill and her husband have vowed to continue holding their international events, framing the scrutiny against them as an unjustified campaign.

sections.text: Engineer David Mummery designed the Swimmer Turbine, a 50kW tidal generator made from fiberglass and steel. sections.text: Unlike utility-scale tidal projects, the ultra-compact turbine can be shipped in a container and built locally without heavy cranes. Anchored invisibly to the seabed, it produces enough electricity for about 30 homes, offering coastal communities direct control over local renewable energy.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Orionid meteor shower has become active as Earth travels through a trail of dust and debris shed by Halley's Comet. Tiny particles enter the atmosphere at around 41 miles per second, creating glowing trails that can briefly linger in the night sky.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The shower peaks overnight from 21 to 22 October, offering up to 20 meteors per hour in dark areas. Rain across the UK is expected to move away early during the peak night, but wetter and windier weather may follow later in the week. Activity continues until 7 November, though light from the approaching full Moon on 26 October may obscure fainter meteors.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: At annual meetings in Bangkok, the World Bank urged developing nations to create specialised small AI models. Chief knowledge officer Paschal Donohoe stated these models operate on mobile phones with low connectivity and in local languages, helping meet specific needs such as agricultural soil analysis in India. Meanwhile, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva called on governments to provide essential preconditions, including electricity, digital infrastructure and safety from bad actors.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Donohoe said economic development that once required centuries could now occur within decades if technology matches local requirements. However, substantial barriers remain; a World Bank report noted that nearly a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lack electricity and over two-thirds lack reliable internet. Georgieva also warned that 40% of global jobs could be augmented or eliminated, severely affecting young workers entering the labour market.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Green Party members voted 1,022 to 813 to approve a motion equating Zionism with racism. Leader Zack Polanski did not vote on the motion but told the BBC he will not overturn it, respecting the democratic will of members. He described Zionism in practical application as racist, argued no state has a right to exist under international law, and denied the motion was controversial, though media outlets noted it caused major fallout.

Green MP Ellie Chowns and others have urged a review of party decision-making rules due to low turnout.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The motion remains party policy for two years until 2028. Polanski aims to amend it at the first available opportunity to support Israelis and Palestinians determining their own future.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Modern romantasy novels follow a tradition of medieval fairy romance that began in French courts during the late 1100s. These popular tales featured adventurous plots, crystal palaces, and sexually active fairies. They circulated widely across Europe before falling out of fashion in the late 1500s as depictions of fairies changed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Both medieval romance and modern romantasy offered safe spaces for women to explore desires free from societal expectations of chastity. The stories frequently inverted conventional gender roles, featuring powerful fairy queens who rescued distressed knights. Despite shaping enduring literature, both historical and contemporary works have faced dismissal and ridicule from critics primarily because women produce and consume them.

stories.title: The problem with telling people the world is ending

articles.title: The problem with telling people the world is ending
articles.standfirst: In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?

timeline.text: The problem with telling people the world is ending

gist: Negative headlines increase online clicks but doom-laden messaging discourages real-world action.
Feelings of dread and helplessness can paralyse the public during serious global crises.
Promoting scientific consensus and hope mobilises people far more effectively than fear.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Researchers evaluated 22,743 headline experiments from Upworthy.com and tested eleven climate messages on 59,440 participants across 63 countries. The analysis showed that while negative wording attracted clicks and doomsday messages were widely shared on social media, frightening texts proved the least effective at encouraging practical efforts to mitigate climate change.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Constant exposure to apocalyptic warnings engenders helplessness rather than motivating change. Inaction becomes a default response when people feel problems are insurmountable. Conversely, sober presentations of scientific consensus and messages emphasising the emotional rewards of action, such as hope and connection, significantly boost real engagement and support for solutions.

fivew: Research examined how negative messaging and doom-laden narratives influence public engagement and action.
The climate messaging study included participants across 63 countries.
To determine which forms of crisis communication effectively mobilise people to take real action.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A kerosene spill spread almost 2.5 miles along the River Taff, affecting areas such as Nantgarw and Taffs Well. Natural Resources Wales located the source on Friday evening and deployed absorbent materials alongside South Wales Fire and Rescue Service to limit fuel entering the water. Residents reported overpowering fumes and dead fish.

sections.text: People were told to close windows and doors as fumes caused eye irritation. One resident reported that up to 25,000 litres had entered the river, while a former fire service protection officer warned that recovery would take years because kerosene does not mix with water.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Officers continue investigating how the fuel reached the drainage system, aiming to stop the pollution completely and collect evidence. Natural Resources Wales is also analysing samples to establish the spill's environmental impact.

timeline.text: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France

gist: Emmanuel Macron called for calm and order after nationwide protests turned into violent riots.
Demonstrations over living costs led to widespread looting and gutted Limoges town hall.
Police arrested around 2,400 people while roughly 1,000 officers were injured during clashes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Around 550,000 demonstrators protested over fuel prices, living costs and deteriorating public services. Rioting, looting and fires erupted across French cities including Paris, Marseille and Limoges, where the historic town hall was gutted by fire. Police arrested roughly 2,400 people, and approximately 1,000 police officers were injured over the weekend.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The violence highlighted deep political divisions in France ahead of April elections. Hard-left and hard-right leaders condemned the government, with accusations traded over police competence and the political exploitation of unrest.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Emmanuel Macron announced that local prefects and mayors would draft measures to safeguard businesses and civic buildings, promising full transparency regarding the police response while offenders face justice.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Following serious policing failures regarding convicted sex offender Simon Levy, the Met launched a pilot scheme using a two-officer female team in north London. Levy killed two women and raped a third who were vulnerable and engaged in street sex work. A previous rape survivor had reported an attack while being arrested, but officers dismissed her and closed the case.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Fear of arrest and lack of trust prevent many street sex workers from reporting severe violence and sexual abuse to authorities. Activists argue that past police crackdowns and ongoing criminalisation create terror among these women and fail to address male violence.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Met plans to expand the specialist approach forcewide if the current pilot successfully builds community confidence.

gist: A man jailed for arson attacks linked to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported.
Fires targeted a car and properties previously or currently linked to the Prime Minister.
A BBC investigation linked the sabotage campaign directly to the Russian state.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: In May 2025, arson attacks targeted sites linked to Sir Keir Starmer while he was prime minister. A previously owned car was set ablaze in Kentish Town, followed by a fire at former flats in Islington, and another at his Kentish Town home rented to his sister-in-law. Lavrynovych and Carpiuc were convicted of conspiring to damage property by fire. A jailed man has since been deported.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A BBC investigation found the arson attacks formed part of a wider campaign of sabotage, provocation, and lies connected to the Russian state. A handler known as EL, suspected to be a young Russian diplomat, directed Lavrynovych and offered Russian citizenship in exchange for further attacks.

fivew: Lavrynovych and Carpiuc were convicted of conspiring to carry out the arson attacks.
Arson attacks targeted properties and a vehicle linked to Sir Keir Starmer.
The fires took place in Kentish Town and Islington.

timeline.text: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?

gist: Sports piracy is surging across Britain as television subscription costs rise significantly.
Broadcasters and authorities are cracking down on illegal streaming services and sellers.
Growing piracy threatens the lucrative financial models of modern professional sports.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Sports piracy has become widespread in the UK, with around half of sports fans admitting to using alternative viewing methods. Authorities recently jailed several individuals for running illegal streaming services and selling unauthorized subscriptions. Meanwhile, millions accessed illicit streams of the Champions League final after it went behind a paywall.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: High subscription costs and the Saturday TV blackout drive fans toward piracy. This illegal viewing costs the broadcasting industry hundreds of millions of pounds annually, threatening the massive rights fees that fund modern sports clubs and grassroots football.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Broadcasters and investigators continue to take down illegal streams while focusing on public education regarding security risks and organized crime links. While current viewer prosecution risks remain low, officials do not rule out tougher policies in the future.

gist: Gloucester and holders Bordeaux Begles drew 36-36 in a thrilling Champions Cup match.
Both teams scored five tries each during the see-saw Pool Three encounter.
A moment of silence was held before kick-off for Lions lock Hyron Andrews.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Gloucester and title holders Bordeaux Begles played out a 36-36 draw at Kingsholm in their Champions Cup opener. The visitors led early through Martin Page-Relo, but Gloucester responded with tries from Arthur Clark, Max Llewellyn and George Barton to lead 24-17 at half-time. Bordeaux hit back through Sipili Falatea, Pablo Uberti and Louis Bielle-Biarrey. Gloucester replacement Will Trenholm scored twice midway through the second half, before Bielle-Biarrey's second try and Maxime Lucu's conversion levelled the match. Neither side could secure a late winner.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Bordeaux, aiming to win the tournament for a third consecutive year, avoided what would have been their first defeat in the competition since April 2024. Before kick-off, players observed a moment's silence following the death of Lions lock Hyron Andrews on Friday at the age of 31.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Lions will play their scheduled fixture against La Rochelle on Saturday in honour of Andrews, with further tributes planned across the opening round of the Champions Cup.

The result marked Scotland's eighth consecutive defeat and fourth in the new competition.
Australia scored eight tries after Scotland took an early fifth-minute lead.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Australia beat Scotland 56-12 in Sydney after scoring eight tries. Katie Buchanan gave Scotland a fifth-minute lead on her first international start, but Australia responded with five tries before half-time.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The defeat was Scotland's eighth in a row. Australia earned their second win of the tournament, with both of their victories coming against the Scots.

sections.text: Liverpool came from behind to secure an away victory against Brentford in the Premier League. gist: Lisandro Martinez criticised Manchester United's board for failing to strengthen the squad.

Manager Michael Carrick stated he needs to investigate the situation before taking action.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: After a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid, defender Lisandro Martinez publicly criticised Manchester United's hierarchy for insufficient investment in the squad. He specifically questioned the technical director, Jason Wilcox, and suggested the club failed to build a strong enough team following their Champions League qualification. The club has struggled recently, failing to win in five matches.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The comments have sparked debate regarding player conduct and club management. Former players Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young argued the public criticism was disrespectful to teammates and could harm dressing room morale. Conversely, some observers and fans feel Martinez's honesty reflects long-standing concerns about recruitment and ownership decisions under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Omar Berrada.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Manager Michael Carrick, who has not yet seen the full interview, indicated he would address the matter after gathering more information. The club faces ongoing pressure regarding its recruitment strategy, financial debt, and the performance of the current squad.
